before: Two participants who split one paragraph at different points at the same time each listed a new paragraph right after it, and Yjs ordered the new paragraphs by client ID. When the paragraph that holds the later tail came first, a moved copy showed in the last paragraph that held it, so the earlier tail showed in the later paragraph, the earlier paragraph showed nothing, and one split looked lost.
after: Paragraphs that a parent lists side by side and that a split added concurrently at one place show in text order. An entry counts as a split's only when the paragraph's split points (collab-split-points) name that entry; a block that a move, an undo, or a redo lists again, and a paragraph without split points, takes no part, so two moves to one place show where their authors put them. Each split's paragraph goes by where the first character its split moved stands in the text it came from; when split points do not decide, paragraphs go by the text they copy: the paragraph whose first copied character comes first in its source text comes first, and when that text is deleted, a paragraph that holds the first character another one copied, after characters of its own, comes first. A paragraph listed later right after one of them, such as a paragraph split off it, moves with it, and only split paragraphs decide where its block shows. A block that an edit moves right after a sibling the rule moves takes that sibling's split points, and when an edit removes such a sibling's entry, the block listed after it from its place takes them, so it keeps the sibling's place; when no block stays after it and the entry it was listed after is removed too, the nearest block that stays between the two takes them, so blocks moved in there keep their place. A run that moves nothing leaves its blocks as listed, and a run inside one of them is read on its own. A block whose entries are all removed shows nothing, so the others order past it. The materializer, the projection of local edits, and the document order that decides where a moved copy shows read this one rule; the projection orders a child it lists right after a moved sibling with that sibling for the rest of the edit. So when two participants split one paragraph at different points at the same time, the new paragraphs show in text order, and later edits land where they show. Each replica reads the order again when the parent's child array changes, even when its ids keep their order, and while a paragraph of the run waits for its text or a named split character.
reason: The rule changes which paragraph shows a moved copy for the same shared state, so it is repair semantics: a replica with repairVersion 2 shows other text in other paragraphs for the same state, and local edits on the two would address different paragraphs. repairVersion increases to 3, so a replica refuses a room that another repair version created before it applies any update. A room created with repairVersion 2 keeps the earlier rules, because only replicas with that version edit it. The rule reads shared state and writes nothing, so no stored field or identity changes. A replica can lack part of that state while updates are on their way: a split point can name a character it has not received. It then orders that run by what it holds, and reads the run again when the character arrives. The clock order of one author decides only when the replica holds both characters and they do not stand in one live text, so every replica that holds the same updates shows the same order, whatever the arrival order and with garbage collection on or off. Tracked concurrent splits still keep one of the proposed paragraph marks on the split paragraph, so one proposed break has no revision and Reject All leaves it; two splits by each peer in one paragraph, a break at the end with a split in the middle, and a redo after both undos are not settled yet.
